rationale: This edition brings the case within the reader's budget. The judgment is restated, not changed. No record in the packet moves a verdict, so the case verdict (unresolved), every claim verdict, the load-bearing set and the weakest links are the incumbent's. The assessment is rewritten field by field within the ceilings, and each header answer now opens with the answer itself. The synthesis keeps the single-record sensitivity (VASO-E020) and names records only beside the claims they are attached to. Two kinds of record are named nowhere in the assessment: provisional records (the relinked essay, report and scanner records) and records drawn from the unverified second essay. Components are restated as six. The electrical nidus becomes its own component, because it carries its own dispute: endplate zone versus tender point. The attention-and-inflammation study stays featured with a full treatment and its incumbent verdict. Selection: three detailed children leave the featured set. The two endplate-noise site findings are carried by their parent claim on the electrical nidus, and the null resistivity index by its parent claim that points differ from their surroundings. Their findings stay in the telling and on their claim pages. Every load-bearing claim, every competing account (latched arteriole, stuck perforator, densification and guarding) and the decisive cruxes remain featured. The article is retold much shorter, as a single pass: phenomenon, instruments, nidus, latch, read path, the three accounts side by side, the breath question, the contemplative maps, what would settle it, and where the case stands. Narration of the case's own revisions and the ledger's internal vocabulary are removed. Claims held only on their sources are told as reports. The breath question is told as a subsection under the three accounts rather than as a fourth account, so the accounts field is unchanged. No research item changed standing, so researchStatus is empty. The question is kept.
article:
Anyone who has leaned on a foam roller knows the small, sharp, oddly specific spots it finds. This case asks what those spots are. One proposal, set out in a self-published essay whose text its author had AI models generate, is that a knot is a *state* rather than a *scar*. On this view it is smooth muscle in a small blood vessel, held in a low-energy “latch,” throttling its patch of tissue until the breath shifts the nervous system and lets it go. More boldly, the proposal says such vascular holds take part in the mind.

What the evidence shows so far: palpated knots differ measurably from nearby tissue, carry a small electrical signal, and respond to mental stress. The latch is real physiology, and slow breathing shifts autonomic balance. What is open: whether anything objective happens in the tissue during a felt release, whether what releases is a vessel at all, and whether the breath matters. The experiments that would decide it are cheap, and none has been run.

## The spot under the roller

The founding essay describes what it says anyone can check: [small, discrete, exquisitely tender points in muscle and fascia]{claim=VASO-C190}, densest at the hips and shoulders and, it adds, more numerous with age. Press in, it says, [breathe out slowly, and something lets go within seconds]{claim=VASO-C004}. It also says [pressure alone, without the breath, does not release the point]{claim=VASO-C039}. That “two-key” rule — pressure to find, exhale to release — is the phenomenon the whole case turns on. It comes from the hypothesis's own proponent and from practitioner lore, and nobody has measured it. It is good evidence that people feel a release, and no evidence that anything happens in the tissue.

The research literature is less sure the spots are even a stable object. A 2009 systematic review found that manual examination for “trigger points,” the clinical name, has never been shown to be reliable, partly because no reference standard exists. A 2015 critique in *Rheumatology* argued that the construct rests on circular reasoning, and drew a rebuttal. [The dispute reaches the observation itself]{claim=VASO-C030}. A 2025 Polish study that imaged runners' calves wrote that “there is no gold standard technique for detecting them.” Its ultrasound confirmed 71.5 percent of the hard spots the examiner had palpated; the rest were tendon or the junction where tendon meets muscle.

[Whether such points are common across the general population]{claim=VASO-C191} has never been measured. The nearest data come from a 1994 survey in two English general practices that used rheumatology's eighteen-site tender-point exam. Its examined sample was chosen for reported pain, so it yields no prevalence figure. Even so, two people who reported no pain at all had eleven or more tender points.

## What the instruments find

Some findings survive the critique. Microdialysis — sampling tissue fluid through a fine probe — found the fluid at active trigger points [more acidic and loaded with mediators of pain and inflammation]{claim=VASO-C005}. The study was small, about nine volunteers, and as its title says, the mediators were raised at sites remote from the points as well as near them.

The most detailed imaging comes from an NIH group in 2011. It imaged 169 sites in the upper trapezius of 44 neck-pain patients. The sonographers were blinded to which sites an examiner had called active (painful on their own), latent (painful only when pressed) or normal. Vibration sonoelastography shakes the tissue and maps where it fails to move. It found a graded stiff region: [about 0.57 square centimetres at active points against 0.36 at latent ones]{claim=VASO-C182}, and [0.17 at palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C187}. Doppler ultrasound found that [arteries within a centimetre or two of active points pulsed more sharply]{claim=VASO-C031}: a pulsatility index of 8.3 against 3.0 near normal sites. At 55 percent of active sites, blood flowed backward between heartbeats.

The same paper carries its own caveats. [Backward flow also appeared near 31 percent of normal sites]{claim=VASO-C032}. A companion resistance index showed no difference at all, and the flow measures could not classify individual sites. There were no pain-free controls: the “normal” sites sat in the same painful muscles. The vessels measured were arteries more than a millimetre across, not the microvessels a latch account needs. And the authors listed three causes for the flow pattern: muscle contracture squeezing the capillary bed, inflammation, and pressure from the probe itself. They did not mention a latch.

A 2025 study of 30 runners' calves found active points larger, stiffer and more painful than latent ones — a parallel in another muscle, again without normal tissue for comparison. So palpated knots are stiffer than their surroundings, in a graded way and inside the muscle, and nearby arteries behave somewhat differently. None of this says what the stiff tissue is.

## A signal the brain can address

In 1993 Hubbard and Berkoff put fine needle electrodes into trapezius trigger points. They found sustained spontaneous electrical activity in a nidus one to two millimetres across, and none in nearby non-tender muscle. A 2002 study qualified that finding. Skeletal muscle receives its nerves in a band called the endplate zone, where faint “endplate noise” is normal. With needles placed by an electrical map of that zone, the noise appeared at all eleven trigger points, at four of eleven non-tender sites inside the zone, and at no site outside it. The fair summary is that [trigger points carry the signal more often than non-tender sites in the same endplate zone, and never where there is no endplate zone]{claim=VASO-C002}. That is a gradient, not an island.

In 1994 McNulty and colleagues kept the electrodes in place in fourteen people and gave them mental arithmetic. [Activity rose at the trigger point while control sites in the same muscle stayed comparatively quiet]{claim=VASO-C003}. A purely mental task turned up the signal at one tender spot. Both studies are small, old and from one research lineage. Neither took a vascular measurement, and neither placed its control needle in a matched endplate-zone site. Three readings are live. The first is stress-sensitive endplates. The second is a sympathetic signal to a vessel inside the muscle. The third, proposed in the proponent's second essay, a source this site has not verified, is [a regional constriction written to a patch of skin, as in blushing or blanching]{claim=VASO-C143}. A skin-perfusion camera over the point during the arithmetic would tell them apart.

A 2026 study in *Nature Human Behaviour* adds a related channel. In preregistered experiments with 57 volunteers, [attending to a histamine skin prick made the inflammation about 1.5-fold smaller and faster to resolve than distraction did, with no change in measures of arousal]{claim=VASO-C006}. It shows that cognition can regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site. It says nothing about knots or seconds: the route was vagal immune regulation, over tens of minutes.

## The ratchet in the vessel wall

{plate:IMG-VASO-P02}

Smooth muscle lines the blood vessels and answers to the autonomic nervous system rather than to the will. Since Hai and Murphy's 1988 model it has been textbook physiology that [it can hold force for long periods at a fraction of the usual energy cost after its activating signal falls]{claim=VASO-C010}. This is the latch-bridge state: motor proteins that have been chemically switched off stay attached and let go only slowly. The signal falls low, not to zero. A cheap hold that outlasts its input is, in engineering terms, a memory element.

The proponents' key clue is the speed of the felt release. Remodelling and scarring take days. [If a point truly releases in seconds, what released was a maintained state, not tissue structure]{claim=VASO-C011}. The inference is sound, but its premise, a measured local event lasting seconds, has never been observed. And “state” is a wide tent. Sustained guarding is a state. So is fascial densification: fascia researchers propose that [thickened hyaluronan between fascial layers thins again under pressure, movement and warmth]{claim=VASO-C077}. If that happens within a session, a knot could be a state without being a vessel. This site has not yet read a primary paper that gives the timescale.

Where has the latch actually been seen? A study run for this case mapped sixteen published experiments by vessel type and size, with three results. First, every measurement of holding cost came from large pig carotid arteries; no arteriole's cost has ever been measured. Second, three studies of pressurized rat skeletal-muscle arterioles, about a tenth of a millimetre across, found that maintained constriction came with maintained or rising activation. In one, the molecular marker of activation rose from 27.7 to 39.6 percent as pressure rose. That is the opposite of the latch signature. Third, the one comparison of an artery with its own branch found latch behaviour in the rabbit femoral artery and a forty-percent loss of held force one branch downstream. The caution cuts both ways: none of the arteriole studies withdrew its stimulus, so none could have seen a hold that outlasts its input. But the compartment the original hypothesis names has been examined, and what was found there does not look like a latch.

## Blood that talks back

In 2008 the neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosa Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis: that [local vascular and blood-flow state can modulate the activity of nearby neurons]{claim=VASO-C012}. In 2024 a *Science* paper showed blood-pressure pulsations modulating neurons in rats through pressure-sensitive ion channels. The read path exists, but as instantaneous nudging in the brain, not as storage.

The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has built a self-published program on these pieces, which he calls vasocomputation. Neural activity writes to vessels, the latch stores what is written, and vessels read it back: [vascular tension as a memory medium in mental life, with the grasping Buddhism calls tanha as its felt signature]{claim=VASO-C021}. The critical report commissioned for this case supplies the sharpest objection. Memory needs a state that depends on past input, can be read out later, and tells different inputs apart. A thermostat has hysteresis without having an autobiography.

## Three accounts side by side

All three live accounts say a knot is a state rather than a scar. They differ over which state, in which tissue, and whether the breath is a key.

### The latched arteriole

On this account, [a knot is an arteriole inside the muscle held shut by latched smooth muscle, starving a small territory, with the acid and the guarding downstream]{claim=VASO-C020}. It would dissolve the old “energy crisis” puzzle: how muscle fibres could stay contracted for years without burning out. It would also explain the breath: pressure perturbs the local loop, and the exhale shifts the chemistry that unlatches. [Slow breathing with long exhalations does reliably shift autonomic balance toward rest]{claim=VASO-C013}, though a 2018 review documents that shift globally, measured at the heart, in people with no tender point under study. The account predicts a stiff, active spot that is metabolically cold on PET, a release blocked by an inhale-and-hold, and [blood returning before stiffness falls]{claim=VASO-C073}. Against it stand the arteriole measurements above, the conduit-sized vessels in the Doppler work, and the absence of any study identifying a latch at a tender point.

### The stuck perforator

The proponent's second essay is AI-written and not yet verified by this site. It accepts the arteriole audit and moves the vessel outward, to the artery-and-nerve bundles that pierce the fascia under the skin. Surgeons call these perforators and find them with a pencil Doppler. On this picture [a knot is held by three things at once: the vessel's tone, a gelled hyaluronan collar around the bundle, and the tether the collar makes to the tissue beneath]{claim=VASO-C174}. Ordinary sympathetic firing would be enough; no latch is needed. The account makes four predictions:

- Tender points sit on Doppler-mapped perforators more often than chance.
- The “star” felt at a release is the tingle of blood returning to one perforator's patch of skin.
- Pressure applied during an inhale-and-hold fails.
- A few millilitres of saline injected around the collar release a knot with no breath at all.

Nothing yet measured bears on the account. It must also explain why the stiff regions sonographers report lie inside muscle rather than under the skin.

### Guarding, densification and interpretation

On this account, tender points are sustained, stress-sensitive motor drive at skeletal endplates under central control, perhaps with densified fascia. The felt release is expectation and attention riding the breath's global calm. The account needs no new physiology, fits the endplate-zone gradient, and gains from the imaging authors' own listing of contracture as a cause of the flow pattern. It predicts that a matched endplate-zone site rises as much as a trigger point under arithmetic, and that pressure alone suffices. It predicts that the sparks felt at release are tingling from overbreathing that tracks carbon dioxide, and that knots are metabolically hot on PET. Its gap is the set of localized, blinded findings a purely central story must still explain: graded stiffness in two muscles, and one spot answering a mental task.

### The breath question

One published protocol comes close to a natural test. The 2025 runners' study released trigger points by thumb compression alone, in thirty-second bouts for up to three rounds, and nothing in its methods mentions breathing. After the first round, 60 percent of active and 86 percent of latent points were no longer visible on ultrasound. This edition reads that as a lead against the two-key rule, not a verdict on it. Breathing was neither instructed, held nor recorded, so a person under painful pressure may have exhaled slowly unprompted. And the treatment lasted minutes, not seconds. What it does show is that an imaged stiff spot can vanish within a single session, which is not how scar behaves.

## The oldest maps

{plate:IMG-VASO-P01}

Tibetan medicine describes channel-knots, rtsa mdud, that breath practice unties; yoga names the granthis; Chinese medicine records ashi points, named for the patient's cry when they are pressed. One reading is that [trained practitioners were mapping the same vascular-autonomic system from inside]{claim=VASO-C022}. The only support is the founding essay's uncited remark that the maps put the important knots along the midline of the torso and in the limbs. No one has coded the traditional locations blind and tested them against anatomy and chance. Until someone does, every match is vulnerable to hindsight.

## What would settle it

The crux is one question. When a knot “releases” on a slow exhale, do stiffness fall and perfusion rise locally, within seconds, beyond what pressure, expectation and general relaxation produce? The keystone experiment would put shear-wave elastography and sensitive Doppler over knots located in advance by blinded examiners, apply calibrated pressure, and record a button press at each felt release. Its controls: pressure without the breath, breath without pressure, an inhale-and-hold, sham sites and failed attempts, plus a mental-arithmetic block. It would cost less than a mid-size grant. The cheapest next step is to repeat the runners' protocol with breathing recorded and randomized — free breathing, slow exhalation, or pressure only during an inhale-and-hold — with sham and untreated points alongside.

What would move the case toward a vascular account:

- Stiffness and perfusion changing together within seconds of the exhale at knots but not sham sites, with blood first.
- An inhale-and-hold blocking the clearance that free or slow breathing achieves.
- Tender points sitting on perforators more often than chance; a knot released by saline at its perforator.
- A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus stops, while its activation marker falls.
- Arithmetic raising the trigger point but not a matched endplate-zone site, or dimming skin perfusion over the point.

What would move it toward the conventional account:

- Felt releases with no reproducible local change, or equal changes at sham sites.
- Equal clearance under held breath, slow exhalation and free breathing.
- Densification reversing under pressure with no change in perfusion.
- Sparks at release that track carbon dioxide and appear equally at sham sites.
- A matched endplate-zone site rising as much as the trigger point under arithmetic.

For the claim about the mind, the test belongs in animals. Do different induced vascular states produce reliably different later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygen supply held constant?

## Where the case stands

The verdict is *unresolved*, and that is a finding. The best-supported pieces are the least decisive: the latch exists, slow breathing shifts autonomic state, vessels nudge neurons, and palpated points are stiffer than their surroundings. Every account predicts them. The pieces that would decide the case have no time-resolved evidence in either direction. The latched-arteriole version is the most exposed, because the arteriole measurements lean against it. The perforator version has nothing behind it yet but its proponent's essay. The conventional account is economical but still owes an explanation of the localized findings.

Proponents have a strong case that this verdict does not answer. The energy-crisis puzzle remains unsolved, and a latch, or a skin vessel the body already keeps constricted, would solve it. A mental task picks out one tender spot. Blinded imaging finds graded stiffness exactly where examiners press. And no one has run the inhale-and-hold arm. The vascular accounts also make a prediction their rival does not — perfusion changing before stiffness — and it is cheap to test.

Someone should film one release. Until then, press into a knot if you find one, and breathe however you like; whether the exhale matters is exactly the question.

assessment.synthesis: The case stays unresolved because its best-evidenced parts decide nothing and its deciding parts are unmeasured. The latch model (VASO-E003, on VASO-C010), slow breathing's autonomic shift (VASO-E009, on VASO-C013) and vascular-to-neural modulation in rat brain (VASO-E005, on VASO-C012) are credible, but guarding and ordinary physiology predict them too. The observation base is real at group level: acidic, mediator-rich chemistry (VASO-E006, on VASO-C005) and graded stiffness at blinded sonography (VASO-E087 and VASO-E089 on VASO-C182; VASO-E090 on VASO-C187). The Doppler signature is partial (VASO-E022 on VASO-C031 and VASO-C032). It is capped by the absence of pain-free controls (VASO-E026) and by a null resistivity index (VASO-E024, on the resistivity claim). The electrical nidus is a prevalence gradient centred on the endplate zone (VASO-E001 and VASO-E031, on VASO-C002). A mental stressor raises it (VASO-E002, on VASO-C003), but against an unmatched control. Palpation is unreliable (VASO-E011, VASO-E010 and VASO-E081, on VASO-C030). Where the original thesis needs the latch, the record points away. On VASO-C020, pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained activation (VASO-E020), no arteriole's holding cost has been measured (VASO-E019), and no latch has been identified at a tender point (VASO-E016). On VASO-C010, latch behaviour vanished one branch downstream in the only paired comparison (VASO-E021). The felt release rests on proponent testimony (VASO-E014, on VASO-C004). The two-key necessity (VASO-C039) has one context record (VASO-E067), which establishes only that a pressure-only protocol gave no breathing instruction. What that protocol achieved is recorded on VASO-C005 (VASO-E072) and is not spent on the two-key claim. Palpable points (VASO-C190) are provisionally supported on sibling imaging records. Their commonness (VASO-C191) has no measuring record: VASO-E108 and VASO-E109 are context. The perforator account, densification's reversibility and the blood-first ordering are held on their sources alone. The memory attribution fails the write–store–read test (VASO-E017). No single removal flips the verdict. Removing VASO-E020 would most change the case, returning the arteriole compartment to unexamined.
assessment.steelman: The classic energy-crisis account has never explained how skeletal fibres stay contracted for years without exhausting themselves. A latch holds tension for almost nothing; and on the perforator proponent's reading, a skin arteriole, which the body already keeps constricted by ordinary tone, would not even need the economy. The electrical nidus is millimetre-scale, and a mental stressor raised it at trigger points while nearby control sites stayed comparatively quiet. Its presence at four of eleven non-tender endplate-zone sites does not explain its presence at eleven of eleven trigger points. Blinded sonographers in two laboratories found stiffer regions exactly where examiners palpated, graded active above latent above normal in the trapezius, and nearby arteries behaved differently. Preregistered experiments show attention regulating a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without any change in arousal — a demonstrated write channel. Every arteriole study showing maintained activation kept its stimulus on, so none could have detected a hold that outlasts its input, which is the only state a knot needs. The one pressure-only protocol neither instructed nor recorded breathing. Proponents argue that people under painful pressure tend to exhale, and the inhale-and-hold arm that would exclude this has not been run. The vascular accounts also predict something their rivals do not — perfusion rising before stiffness falls — and it is cheap to test. None of this shows that knots are vessels; it is why the verdict cannot close against them.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Muscle knots are maintained vascular-autonomic states, not damaged tissue — in the graded form, latched microvascular smooth muscle throttling local flow, with guarding on top, released by pressure plus slow exhalation. Admitted evidence carries the surroundings: palpated points differ in chemistry, graded stiffness and partly in flow; a stress-sensitive electrical nidus; the latch in conduit arteries; slow breathing's global effect. The breath's necessity and a skin-perforator variant are held on their sources alone; vascular memory in the mind rests on hypothesis statements.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: The crux is whether anything objective happens locally when a knot 'releases' on a slow exhale — stiffness falling and perfusion rising within seconds, beyond pressure, expectation and global relaxation. Behind it sit three disputes. Which tissue holds the state: an intramuscular arteriole (where measurements show maintained activation, not latch), a skin perforator (unmeasured), stress-sensitive endplates, or fascial hyaluronan? Is the breath a key at all, given a pressure-only protocol that cleared imaged points with breathing uninstructed? And can palpation reliably find the points?
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A time-locked imaging study of single releases would settle it: elastography and sensitive Doppler over blinded-located knots, with pressure-only, breath-only, inhale-hold and sham controls. Stiffness and perfusion changing together within seconds of the exhale, blood first, beyond all controls, would favour a vascular state; felt releases with no local change would return knots to guarding. Cheaper companions: the runners' compression protocol repeated with breathing randomised, a blinded tender-point-to-perforator map, and a paired-caliber arteriole study with stimulus withdrawal.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Tender points are neuromuscular guarding: sustained, centrally maintained, stress-sensitive motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, possibly with densified fascial hyaluronan. The electrical signature is endplate noise, commoner where tissue is tender and present at some non-tender endplate-zone sites; a stressor raising drive to endplates raises it. The stiff region sonographers map is contracted fibre, graded with symptoms. The acidic chemistry and high-resistance Doppler waveforms follow from contracture compressing the bed, which the imaging authors themselves list as a cause, while a second resistance index shows no difference at all. Pressure switches guarding off or thins the lubricant. That is why a compression protocol with breathing uninstructed made most imaged points undetectable within minutes. The felt release on an exhale is expectation and attention riding slow breathing's global parasympathetic shift. Poor palpation reliability means part of the observation base may be artifact. The account's gap is the localized, blinded, instrumented findings a purely central story must still explain.

components.label: The observation base: palpable points that differ from surrounding tissue
components.note: Graded stiffness at blinded sonography, altered chemistry and a partial Doppler signature at group level; palpation is unreliable and commonness unmeasured.

components.label: The electrical nidus and its address
components.note: Stress-sensitive activity, commoner at trigger points but centred on the endplate zone; old, small, one lineage, no matched control.

components.label: The latch, where shown and where needed
components.note: Real in conduit arteries; pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained activation, and no arteriole's holding cost has been measured.

components.label: The breath key and the seconds-scale release
components.note: The felt release rests on testimony; the breath's necessity is untested; only the global autonomic shift is established.

components.label: Vascular memory and the mind
components.note: The read path is shown in rat brain; no write–store–read demonstration exists in any mammalian vessel.

components.label: Competing mechanisms: perforator, densification, guarding
components.note: Perforator and densification are held on their sources alone; guarding needs no new physiology but must explain the localized findings.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive experiments are cheap, specified and unrun; one imaging study, or one breath-randomised repeat of an existing protocol, would move the central verdict in either direction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Stated only as hypothesis (VASO-E013, VASO-E038, both context). The write–store–read criterion set out in VASO-E017 is unmet: no study shows a vascular state storing input and later returning it to neurons. Its parts are separately credible, but that is a prior, not evidence for the composite. Unresolved rather than contradicted, because nothing has tested it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tension in blood vessels acts as a kind of memory that takes part in thought and in the 'clinging' Buddhism describes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A demonstrated vascular memory would separate vasocomputation from ordinary neurovascular plumbing; nothing now bears on it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Hysteresis is not memory, and a vascular effect on neurons may be nonspecific perfusion change.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An animal study in which different induced vascular states produce reliably different later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygenation clamped.
A clean negative: vascular manipulation altering neural gain only through instantaneous perfusion.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Its statements (VASO-E013, VASO-E037) are context. In the compartment it names, pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising activation rather than a latch (VASO-E020). No arteriole's holding cost has been measured (VASO-E019), and no latch has been identified at a tender point (VASO-E016). The one supporting flow record (VASO-E027) fits compression equally well. Not contradicted: no arteriole study withdrew its stimulus to test holding without input.

treatment.plainLanguage: A knot is a small blood vessel inside the muscle held shut by smooth muscle in its low-energy latch.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shown at a tender point, it would decide the case for the vascular account; excluded, knots return to guarding or the vessel moves elsewhere.
treatment.strongestObjection: Where arteriolar constriction has been measured, it tracks sustained activation, not a latch.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after stimulus withdrawal while its activation marker falls.
A stiff, electrically active knot that is metabolically cold on FDG-PET.
Perfusion rising before stiffness falls at a timed release.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its one source, the proponent's second essay, which this site has not verified; no evidence record bears on it. It is catalogued as an alternative to the latch reading, not as a finding, and grades unresolved for that reason alone.

treatment.plainLanguage: A knot is a vessel-and-nerve bundle under the skin, held stuck by vessel tone, a gelled collar and a fascial tether.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Its predictions — tender points on perforators, release by saline without breath, block under inhale-hold — diverge sharply from the rivals' and are cheap to test.
treatment.strongestObjection: Blinded sonography locates the stiff regions inside muscle, not in the fascia under the skin.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded tender points coinciding with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance.
Saline hydrodissection at a mapped perforator releasing a tender point with no breath.
Coincidence no better than chance.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only record (VASO-E039) is the founding essay's uncited remark on where traditional maps place knots, with no coding rule or chance baseline. No blinded comparison of traditional locations with anatomy exists.

treatment.plainLanguage: Traditional maps of bodily knots record the same vascular-autonomic system, felt from inside.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a genuine alignment with vascular geography would bear on the maps, not on whether anything latches.
treatment.strongestObjection: Flexible traditional locations invite post-hoc matching to anatomy.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered blind coding of rtsa mdud, granthi and ashi locations aligning with vascular or autonomic anatomy above chance.
A null alignment under the same design.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The Hai–Murphy model (VASO-E003) reproduces high sustained force at low phosphorylation and is textbook physiology. The one paired femoral–saphenous comparison (VASO-E021) qualifies its generality: latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream. The essay's restatement (VASO-E034) adds nothing and overstates the model.

treatment.plainLanguage: Smooth muscle in vessels can keep holding tension cheaply after the signal that tightened it fades.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every account accepts it; it shows the mechanism exists, not that it acts at knots.
treatment.strongestObjection: Demonstrated in conduit arteries and not generic across vessel types.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replicated loss of latch behaviour across successive downstream vessel orders would narrow its reach further.
Evidence that latched force requires continuing activation in the preparations where it was described.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A conditional claim: if a release is objective within seconds, what released is a state. The support is a physiological prior, stated as such: structural remodelling takes days. The essay's argument (VASO-E035) restates that prior. A small needling pilot (VASO-E030, context) shows the measures move over visits, not seconds. The premise remains untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: If a knot really lets go in seconds, it was something the body was doing, not damaged tissue.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Separates state from scar, but every live account already says state; it does not pick which one.
treatment.strongestObjection: The premise — an objective seconds-scale release — has never been observed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Time-resolved imaging showing an objective local change within seconds of a felt release.
Evidence of structural change on a seconds timescale, which would break the inference.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on the founding essay's statement of the Stecco group's proposal. The primary densification papers have not been retrieved, and no evidence record bears on the claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: Thickened lubricant between fascial layers loosens again with pressure, movement and warmth.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If it reverses within a session, pressure alone could release a knot with no vascular change — a direct rival to both vascular accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: Its timescale is unknown, and much of the densification evidence is anatomical or cadaveric.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A measured reversal of fascial viscosity or glide under pressure within seconds to minutes.
Stiffness dropping at a release with no perfusion change.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Blood-pressure pulsations modulating neurons through mechanosensitive channels in rat preparations and awake animals (VASO-E005) is strong direct evidence for the direction; the hypothesis paper (VASO-E004) is context. The grade is provisional because the effect is shown in rat brain and is instantaneous, not shown in peripheral tissue or for stored states.

treatment.plainLanguage: The state of blood vessels can change what nearby nerve cells do.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The vascular accounts need it, but ordinary physiology predicts it too; it shows reading, not storage.
treatment.strongestObjection: Brain-only and instantaneous; it says nothing about knots.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A peripheral demonstration of vessel-to-sensory-neuron modulation.
Failure to replicate the mechanosensitive effect.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A systematic review (VASO-E009) documents reproducible rises in heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia with slow breathing in healthy people. The essay's assertion (VASO-E036) adds nothing. The evidence is global and cardiac; nothing measures local tissue.

treatment.plainLanguage: Slow breathing with long exhalations shifts the nervous system toward its resting mode.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every account accepts the global shift; the site-specific unlatching added on top is unmeasured.
treatment.strongestObjection: Global cardiac indices say nothing about a local event at a tender point.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Local perfusion at a tender point rising time-locked to exhalation and absent at sham sites.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A systematic review found manual trigger-point examination unreliable and without a reference standard (VASO-E011). A peer-reviewed critique contests the construct (VASO-E010). A 2025 clinical group states the palpation variability and reports that imaging confirmed 71.5% of palpated spots (VASO-E078, VASO-E079, VASO-E081). The NIH imaging group concedes the reference standard is subjective (VASO-E029). The critique was answered, but the reliability point stands.

treatment.plainLanguage: Examiners cannot reliably agree where trigger points are, and whether they are a real entity is debated.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It weakens the observation base every account explains rather than favouring one account.
treatment.strongestObjection: Localization by instrument may escape the palpation problem.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded, instrument-defined localization with good agreement between examiners.
Imaging confirming nearly all palpated points across laboratories.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Its own records are context only: two pain-free people with eleven or more fixed-site tender points in a pain-selected sample (VASO-E082), and a literature colloquialism (VASO-E109). The grade leans, disclosed, on sibling records. Blinded sonography found graded stiff regions at palpated sites (VASO-E087 on VASO-C182; VASO-E090 on VASO-C187), and imaging confirmed most palpated spots (VASO-E081 on VASO-C030). Palpation's unreliability keeps the grade provisional.

treatment.plainLanguage: You can press and find small, sharply tender spots in muscle and fascia.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every account starts from it; it decides nothing between them.
treatment.strongestObjection: In one study about a quarter of palpated 'knots' were tendon or tendon-muscle junction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded agreement between examiners confirmed by imaging.
Imaging finding no correlate at most palpated spots.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record counts tender points in unselected people. The two records on the claim are context: a 1986 clinic estimate for myofascial pain quoted second-hand (VASO-E108), and the phrase 'commonly recognized as muscle knots' (VASO-E109). The 1994 pain-free individuals (VASO-E082) sit in a pain-selected sample. Commonness is simply unmeasured.

treatment.plainLanguage: Such tender spots are common in ordinary people.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Bears on the scale of the phenomenon, not on its mechanism.
treatment.strongestObjection: No census of tender points has ever been taken.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An unselected population survey with blinded examination and imaging.
Retrieved community tender-point surveys reporting count distributions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Hubbard and Berkoff found sustained activity in a 1–2 mm nidus at every trigger point and none at non-tender sites (VASO-E001). Simons 2002 (VASO-E031) found the noise at 11/11 trigger points, 4/11 non-tender endplate-zone sites and 0/11 off-zone taut bands, turning an island into a gradient. The studies are small, old and unblinded, with proponent authors. The essay restatements (VASO-E043, VASO-E052) carry no weight.

treatment.plainLanguage: Trigger points show a tiny spot of ongoing electrical activity, more often than nearby non-tender muscle does.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows knots are electrically maintained, but its tie to the endplate zone fits a skeletal-endplate reading as well as a vascular one.
treatment.strongestObjection: Endplate noise also occurs outside trigger points within the endplate zone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A modern blinded replication with matched endplate-zone controls.
A retrieved primary study showing sympathetic blockade quiets the nidus.

claimAssessments.reasoning: In fourteen subjects, mental arithmetic raised needle-EMG activity at trigger points while control sites stayed comparatively quiet (VASO-E002). The study comes from one lineage and was never replicated with modern instruments. It took no vascular measure, and its control was not a matched endplate-zone site. The essay's restatement (VASO-E033) adds nothing.

treatment.plainLanguage: A purely mental task turns up the electrical activity at a trigger point but not nearby.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows central addressing of one spot, but the endplate, intramuscular-vessel and skin-vessel readings all fit it.
treatment.strongestObjection: With an unmatched control, the stressor may simply raise activity in any endplate zone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A repeat with a matched endplate-zone control: a selective rise restores localization, an equal rise removes it.
A fall in skin perfusion over the point during the arithmetic.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on the proponent's second essay, which this site has not verified; no evidence record bears on it.

treatment.plainLanguage: The mental-stress effect at a knot is the nervous system constricting the vessels of one patch of skin, as in blushing or blanching.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Would move the address from muscle to skin, favouring the perforator account over the latched arteriole.
treatment.strongestObjection: The stress signal was recorded by intramuscular skeletal EMG; no skin measure was taken.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A localized fall in skin perfusion over a tender point during mental arithmetic, absent over control skin.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supported only by first-person and practitioner testimony from the hypothesis's proponent, in an essay whose text was AI-generated (VASO-E014). It is real evidence that people feel releases, but no tissue change has been measured, and expectation and attention cannot be excluded.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pressing a knot while breathing out slowly makes it feel as if it lets go within seconds.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: As testimony it cannot separate a local event from interpretation; its value lies in what a measurement of it would show.
treatment.strongestObjection: A felt release is exactly what expectation plus global relaxation would produce.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Button-pressed felt releases coinciding with objective local changes in stiffness and perfusion.
Felt releases occurring equally at sham sites.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on the founding essay's statement. Its one evidence record (VASO-E067) is context: a published pressure-only protocol neither gave nor recorded any breathing instruction. What that protocol achieved is recorded against another claim and is not counted here. Breathing was uncontrolled, and the course ran minutes, not seconds.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pressure alone, without the slow exhale, won't release a knot.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The breath's necessity separates the vascular accounts (breath-gated) from guarding (pressure suffices); a breath-randomised trial would decide it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Runners' trigger points became undetectable under compression with breathing uninstructed — suggestive, though not a controlled test.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An inhale-and-hold failing to clear points that free or slow breathing clears.
Equal clearance under held, slow and free breathing.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on the founding essay's statement of a prediction. No timed release has been imaged in any tissue, and no evidence record bears on the claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: When a knot releases, blood flow returns first and stiffness drops after.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A distinctive timing signature: perfusion leading stiffness favours a vascular account; stiffness change without perfusion favours guarding or densification.
treatment.strongestObjection: The ordering is unobserved and may sit below the time resolution of current imaging.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Time-resolved elastography and Doppler showing perfusion leading stiffness across release events.
Stiffness change leading, or no perfusion change at all.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Acidic, mediator-rich fluid at active points (VASO-E006; about nine subjects; also at remote sites). Blinded vibration sonoelastography separates active, latent and normal sites (VASO-E087, VASO-E090, VASO-E091, VASO-E096, VASO-E099, VASO-E100, VASO-E102). There is a group-level Doppler difference (VASO-E022) and a second-hand review (VASO-E007). All are capped by the absence of pain-free controls (VASO-E026) and by flow indices that do not classify sites (VASO-E025). The calf findings (VASO-E071, VASO-E072) are context.

treatment.plainLanguage: Active trigger points differ from surrounding tissue in chemistry, stiffness and blood flow.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Real group-level differences that every account can explain; nothing says what the altered tissue is.
treatment.strongestObjection: Sites were palpation-selected, the work comes from one laboratory lineage, and there were no pain-free controls.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The differences confirmed at instrument-defined sites against pain-free controls in an independent laboratory.
The differences vanishing once pain-free controls are added.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Preregistered within-subject experiments in 57 volunteers found attention to a histamine prick gave about 1.5-fold smaller, faster-resolving responses in about 90% across two cohorts, with arousal measures unchanged (VASO-E008). Single laboratory, very recent, mediators not measured. The essay's caveat (VASO-E041) limits its reach: the route is vagal, over tens of minutes.

treatment.plainLanguage: Paying attention to an inflamed patch of skin makes the inflammation smaller and quicker to fade, without any rise in arousal.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An existence proof that cognition can regulate a vascular bed at a chosen site; it says nothing about knots, latches or seconds-scale release.
treatment.strongestObjection: The route is vagal immune regulation over tens of minutes in healthy skin, not a vascular hold at a tender point.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication in another laboratory.
A comparable attention effect on perfusion or stiffness at a tender point.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A median pulsatility index of 8.3 near active points against 3.0 near normal sites (VASO-E022), from one blinded-sonographer study, capped by the absence of pain-free controls (VASO-E026). The vessels were arteries over a millimetre across, not microvessels.

treatment.plainLanguage: Arteries next to active trigger points pulse more sharply than arteries near normal spots.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: High downstream resistance fits a clenched vessel and contracture compressing the bed alike.
treatment.strongestObjection: The authors themselves list compression, inflammation and probe pressure as causes.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replication with pain-free controls and microvascular imaging.
The index difference disappearing under controlled probe pressure.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Backward diastolic flow near 31% of palpably normal sites (VASO-E022), within symptomatic muscle and with no pain-free controls (VASO-E026). It makes the waveform a gradient rather than a marker of a knot.

treatment.plainLanguage: The backward-flow pattern also shows up near about a third of normal-feeling spots.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cuts against the waveform as a knot signature without favouring any mechanism.
treatment.strongestObjection: The rate may reflect spillover from nearby trigger points rather than a baseline.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Rates of retrograde flow in pain-free controls.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Mean stiff areas of 0.57 cm² at active and 0.36 cm² at latent sites on blinded vibration sonoelastography (VASO-E087, VASO-E089, VASO-E104). The calf parallel and further listings are context (VASO-E085, VASO-E093, VASO-E106). One laboratory, one vibration frequency, palpation-selected sites.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stiff regions are larger at points painful on their own than at points painful only when pressed.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A graded stiffness ordering that all accounts can accommodate.
treatment.strongestObjection: The site classes are defined by the same palpation whose reliability is disputed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication with instrument-defined sites.
The gradient disappearing under blinded site selection.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Palpably normal sites measured 0.17 ± 0.22 cm² (VASO-E090, VASO-E104, VASO-E105, VASO-E107), well below trigger-point sites. The normal sites lay in symptomatic muscle, and there were no pain-free controls.

treatment.plainLanguage: Normal-feeling spots in the same muscles had much smaller stiff areas.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Supplies the comparison that makes the stiffness gradient; does not decide the mechanism.
treatment.strongestObjection: Wide variance, and the 'normal' tissue sits in painful muscle.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Pain-free control values from an independent laboratory.
